1:1:
Chap. I. 1–18.] Prologue: in which is contained the substance and subject of the whole Gospel. The Eternal Word of God, the source of all existence, life, and light, became flesh, dwelt among us, was witnessed to by John, rejected by His own people, but received by some, who had power given them to become the sons of God. He was the perfection and end of God's revelation of Himself; which was partially made in the law, but fully declared in Jesus Christ.

1–5.] The eternal pre-existence of the λόγος: His personal distinctness; but essential unity with God. His working in creation, and in the enlightening of men, before His manifestation in the flesh; His non-apprehension by them.

1.] Before commencing on the truths here declared, it is necessary to discuss the one word on which the whole turns: viz. ὁ λόγος. This term is used by John without explanation, as bearing a meaning well known to his readers. The enquiry concerning its meaning must therefore be conducted on historical, not on mere grammatical, grounds. The most important elements of the enquiry are, (I.) the usage of the word, by John himself and other biblical writers: and (II.) the purely historical information which we possess on the ideas attached to the word.

(α) From the first consideration we find, that in other biblical authors, as well as in John, the word is never used to signify the divine Reason or Mind; nor indeed those of any human creature. These ideas are expressed by πνεῦμα or καρδία, or νοῦς, or ῃ σοφία τοῦ θεοῦ. In the classics λόγος never signifies the subjective faculty of reason. The usual meaning of λόγος is speech, or word.

(β) That this is also the import of this prologue is manifest, from the evident relation which it bears to the opening of the history of creation in Genesis.

(γ) Again, this λόγος in our prologue is not personal merely as an abstraction, nor as a personification, — not the spoken word of God, once manifested in the prophets but afterwards more fully declared in Christ, as Luthardt (i. 280 ff.) maintains, comparing Heb. i. 1, — but a PERSON: for ὁ λόγος ἦν πρός τὸν θεόν, and ὁ λόγος ἔγένετο: also θεός ἦν ὁ λόγος. I cannot consent to disconnect the use of λόγος by St. John from its previous history. That this use, as a matter of fact, was prepared by the Alexandrine philosophy, is no way affected by the difference between the λόγος of St. John and that of Philo, and the corrupt character of that philosophy itself.

II. (α) We are now to enquire, how it came that St. John found this word λόγος so ready made to his hands, as to require no explanation. The answer will be found by tracing the gradual personification of the Word, or Wisdom, of God, in the Old Testament and Jewish writings.

(β) We find faint traces of this personification in the book of Psalms: see Ps. xxxiii. 4, 6; cxix. 89, 105; cvii. 20; cxlvii. 15, 18. But it was not the mere offspring of poetic diction; for the whole form and expression of the Old Testament revelation was that of the Word of God. The Mosaic History opens with ‘God said, Let there be light.’ Spoken commands, either openly or in visions, were the communications from God to man. It is the Word, in all the Prophets; the Word, in the Law; in short, the Word, in all God's dealings with His people.

(γ) And as the Word of God was the constant idea for His revelations relatively to man, so was the Wisdom of God, for those which related to His own essence and attributes. His Almightiness was first felt, before His Wisdom and moral Purity were appreciated. In the book of Job (ch. xxviii. 12 ff.) and the Proverbs (ch. viii., ix.) we find this Wisdom of God personified; in the latter in very plain and striking terms, ascribing to it personal action and pre-existence before the creation of the world.

(δ) Further evidences of this gradual personification are found in the two Apocryphal Books, the Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, and the Wisdom of Solomon. In Sirach, ch. i. 1, Wisdom is said to be παρά κυρίου, καί μετῒ αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα: and in ver. 4, προτέρα πάντων ἔκτισται σοφία. In the Wisdom of Solomon (ch. vi. 22–ch. ix.) a similar personification and eulogy of Wisdom occurs: Wisdom is called πάρεδρος τῶν σῶν θρόνων (ch. ix. 4), and is said to have been παροῦσα ὅτε ἐποίεις τὸν κόσμον (ch. ix. 9); and in ch. xviii. 15, 16, the παντοδύναμος λόγος is set forth as an Angel coming down from heaven, and destroying the Egyptians.

It is highly probable that the authors of these books, in adopting such expressions, were acquainted with the Alexandrine philosophy, in which the λόγος or σοφία of God had assumed a half-personal, half-attributive character — which philosophy, by the time St. John wrote, had prepared the way for his use of the term, without his being in any way dependent upon, or identified with, its peculiar tenets.

ἦν, καί ὁ λ. ἦν πρός τ. θ.] The usage of πρός here, as with (i.e. ‘chez’), is sufficiently borne out by the reff. John says πρός τὸν θεόν, not ἐν τῶ θεῶ, in order that he might not give occasion to a confusion of the (divine) Persons. Both the inner substantial union, and the distinct personality of the λόγος, are here distinctly asserted. The former is distinctly repeated in the next words, καί θεός ἦν ὁ λόγος, and the Word was God.

καί θεός ἦν ὁ λ.] As regards the form of the sentence, it is strictly parallel here as with ch. iv. 24. But the sense forbids us to render it as though it meant ‘and God was the Word’; for what meaning could such an assertion possibly convey? It would be a contradiction to the distinction just drawn between God and the Word. Nor would this only be the case, but the assertion would be inconsistent with the whole historical idea of the λόγος, reducing the term to a mere attribute of God, as when it is said ὁ θεός ἀγάπη ἐστίν. The omission of the article before θεός is not mere usage: ὁ λόγος ἦν ὁ θεός would give a sense liable to the objection just stated, and would destroy the idea of the λόγος altogether. θεός must then be taken as implying God in substance and essence, — not ὁ θεός, ‘the Father,’ in Person. As σάρξ ἐγένετο (ver. 14) expresses the state into which the Divine Word entered by a definite act, so θεός ἦν expresses that essence which was His ἐν ἀρχῇ: He was very God. So that this first verse is thus connected: that the Logos was from eternity, — was Himself with God (the Father), — and was Himself God.
1:3: 3.] τὰ πάντα, equivalent to πάντα in 1 Cor. vi. 6, Col. i. 16, ≡ ὁ κόσμος of ver. 10. This parallelism of itself refutes the Socinian interpretation of πάντα as ‘all Christian grace and virtues,’ or ‘the whole moral world.’ The history of the use of λόγος forbids such an explanation utterly: Philo himself speaks of the λόγος of God as the instrument by which the universe was framed (compare Col. i. 16, and Heb. i. 2). This statement is not merely a Hebraistic parallelism, but a distinct denial of the eternity and uncreatedness of matter as held by the Gnostics, who set matter, as a separate existence, over against God, making it the origin of evil — a notion which John here excludes. Nothing was made without Him (the λόγος); all things, all matter, came into being διῒ αὐτοῦ. The punctuation at the end of the verse is uncertain, so far as manuscript authority alone is concerned; but the sense of the passage is both weakened, and rendered inconsistent with analogy, by placing the full stop after οὐδὲ ἕν, and reading ὅ γέγονεν with what follows.
1:4: 4.] ἐν αὐτῷ ζωή ἦν, καί ῃ ζωή ἦν τὸ φῶς τῶν ἀνθρώπων. The life which was in Him was not bare existence, but that life of which He is the eternal fountain, communicated to created beings; and this life, imparted to the reasonable creature, man, became his light, his guide to the knowledge of God.
1:5: 5.] καί τὸ φῶς ἐν τῇ σκοτία φαίνει, καί ῃ σκοτία αὐτὸ οὐ κατέλαβεν. Not merely the σκοτία spoken of in Eph. iv. 18, but the whole mass of fallen humanity, with the sole exception (see below, ver. 12) of ὅσοι ἔλαβον αὐτόν. This φαίνει is not merely an historical present, but describes the whole process of the light of life in the Eternal Word shining in this evil and dark world; both by the Old Testament revelations, and by all the scattered fragments of light glittering amid the darkness of heathendom. κατέλαβεν, comprehended, apprehended: John here states, as a general fact, what he afterwards states of the historical appearance of the Incarnate Word among His chosen people (ver. 11) — the sentences are strictly parallel: τὸ φῶς ἐν τῇ σκοτία φαίνει corresponds to εἰς τὰ ἰδια ἦλθεν, and ῃ σκοτία αὐτὸ οὐ κατέλαβεν corresponds to οἱ ἰδιοι αὐτὸν οὐ παρέλαβον. In the first, the rejection by the world in general; in the second, the historical rejection by the Jews. The connexion of the two clauses by καί is not ‘and therefore,’ as though darkness must by its nature exclude light, but ‘and yet’ — notwithstanding the light's presence and effect — the darkness comprehended it not.
1:6:
6–18.] The manifestation and working of the Divine Word, Christ, the Son of God, incarnate in our flesh.

6.] The Evangelist now passes on to the historic manifestation of the Word. He enunciates briefly in this and the next verse what he afterwards, ver. 19–36, narrates at length. No stress is to be laid on ἔγένετο as distinguished from ἰν ἄνθρωπος in ch. iii. 1: there was a man sent, &c. In ἀπεσταλμένος παρὲ θεοῦ we have a probable reference to Mal. iii. 1.
1:7: 7.] The purpose of John's coming was to bear witness to a fact — a fact made known to him by divine revelation (ver. 33). εἰς μαρτυρίαν: for witness. ἔνα μαρτ. is an expansion of this: the subject of his testimony was to be the Light, and the aim of it that all might believe through him (i.e. through John); not τοῦ φωτός, for then we should need εἰς before θεόν after πιστεύ., which is here out of place.
1:8: 8.] John was himself a lamp, burning and shining (ch. v. 35), but not the Light itself. The word here rendered Light imports the original, archetypal, true source and pattern of those things which we find here below in fragmentary imitations and derivations.
1:9: 9.] τὸ φῶς τὸ ἀληθινόν is not opposed here to ‘false,’ but to that which is partial or derivative: the Logos is light κατῒ ἔξοχήν, the only original and underived source of all spiritual illumination given to man, lighting every man that cometh into the world.
1:10: 10.] The κόσμος here, into which He came (ver. 9), was made by Him (ver. 3); nevertheless — His own creature, unrecognizing — the world knew Him not. αὐτόν, not αὐτό, because the masculine brings in again the creative λόγος, who is the Light. The three members of the sentence form a climax: He was in the world (and therefore the world should have known Him); and the world was made by Him (much more then should it have known Him); and the world knew Him not.
1:11: 11.] τὰ ἰδια cannot mean the world in general here; it would be difficult to point out any scriptural usage so general. The analogy of other passages favours the meaning which makes τὰ ἰδια His own inheritance or possession, i.e. Judæa; compare Matt. xxi. 33 ff. and Sir. xxiv. 7 ff. And thus ἦλθεν is a step nearer the declaration in ver. 14, He came to His own. On παρέλαβον see above on ver. 5.
1:14: Two pages are missing from this scan of the source at exactly this point (the text jumps from the close of verse 14's opening clause to the middle of a sentence on verse 15) — Alford's notes on the rest of verse 14 are not available here.
1:15: See note on v. 14 (also affected by the missing pages). What survives picks up mid-discussion: John's witness, ‘He that cometh after me is preferred before me, for he was before me,’ is explained as referring to dignity and pre-existence, not to the order of birth — John's own course was already being fulfilled when he made way for the advancement of Christ to His office, even though the Baptist had been born first in the flesh.
1:16: 16.] τὸ πλήρωμα is that of which He was πλήρης, ver. 14, and is not connected with the Gnostic πλήρωμα. ἡμεῖς πάντες: all who believe on Him, see ver. 12. ἐλάβομεν, καί: received, and — our relation to Him has been that of recipients of His fulness. χάριν ἀντὶ χάριτος: the old interpretation, ‘the new covenant instead of the old’ (Euthym.), is certainly wrong; the sense is rather grace upon grace — new grace coming upon and superseding the former, continual and successive, ever fresh, like the manna, day by day, this taking the place of that.
1:17: 17.] The connexion of this verse with the foregoing lies in the words χάριν ἀντὶ χάριτος (ver. 16): we received from His fulness continual additional gifts, like the law — a positive enactment, finite and circumscribed, of which it could be said that it ἐδόθη, was given; but ἡ χάρις καί ἡ ἀλήθεια διὰ Ἀησοῦ χριστοῦ ἐγένετο, grace and truth came, were brought into being, by Jesus Christ. The distinction is not between the narrowness of positive enactment in the law and the largeness of the Gospel: it is between ἐδόθη and ἐγένετο — between the giving of a code and the bringing in of a Person.
1:18:
18.] No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son (some of the oldest authorities read ‘the only begotten God’), which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him. οὐδεὶς ἕωρακεν πώποτε: no man hath ever seen God — not even Moses, who spoke with God face to face (Exod. xxxiii. 11), saw Him as He is. But there is One who can declare Him: He who is, abides, in the bosom of the Father — the closest possible relation of love and knowledge — hath declared Him, in the fullest sense.

[The reading ‘only begotten Son’ versus ‘only begotten God’ is the subject of an extended critical note weighing patristic citations on both sides — Tertullian, Hippolytus, the Synodical Epistle of the Council of Antioch, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Didymus, Basil, Cyril of Alexandria, Eusebius, Hilary, and Athanasius are all cited and discussed at length. That apparatus is condensed here rather than reproduced in full.]
1:19:
19–28.] First witness borne by John to Jesus: by deputation from the Sanhedrim.

19, 20.] The deputation sent was a formal one — priests and Levites, the two classes of persons employed about the service of the temple (see Josh. iii. 3) — sent to enquire of him concerning the pretensions of the new Teacher (ver. 25), who had collected such multitudes about him (Luke iii. 15), and had awakened popular expectation that he was the Messiah; and this in an unbelieving and inquisitorial spirit, compare Matt. iii. 7 ff. Even among the learned, as well as among the people, there were considerable differences as to the prophecies respecting the Messiah: see ch. xii. 40–52.

20.] ὁμολόγησεν, by formal confession. This emphatic notice of his denial is introduced not to guard against too high an estimate of John's work and office, but rather to shew the importance of his testimony, which was so publicly and officially delivered, and the way in which he declared himself in comparison with Him who came after him.
1:21: 21.] Ἔλίας εἶ σύ;] The reference is not to the usual expectation of Elias coming bodily down from heaven as forerunner and anointer of the Messiah (our Lord refers to this sense in Matt. xi. 14, εἰ θέλετε δέξασθαι, αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ μέλλων ἔρχεσθαι); in this sense John was not Elias, though in the spirit and power of Elias he was (Luke i. 17). ὁ προφήτης εἶ σύ;] From the prophecy of Moses, Deut. xviii. 15, 18, the Jews expected some particular prophet to arise, distinct from the Messiah (a distinction not held by all, see ch. vi. 14), whose coming was, like that of Elias, intimately connected with the Messiah's own: see ch. xx. 40, 41; and compare Matt. xvi. 14, where 'Jeremiah, or one of the prophets' seems to be this same expected figure, generally held to be one of the old prophets raised from the dead (see also 2 Macc. ii. 1–8). This John was not, and he answers accordingly in the negative.
1:22: 22.] Notice: they ever ask about his person; he ever refers them to his office. He is no one — a voice merely: it is the work of God, the testimony to Christ, which is every thing. So the formalist in the church always asks, Who is he? while the true witness for Christ only exalts and cares for Christ's work.
1:23: 23.] These words, by which the Evangelist relates the testimony of John, appear from this place to have been first used by himself. They introduce the great closing section of the prophecy of Isaiah (ch. xl.–lxvi.), so full of the rich promises and revelations of the Messiah and His Kingdom, here compendiously expressed by εὐθύνατε τὴν ὁδόν κυρίου. By implication, the Baptist, in quoting this opening of the section, announces the approaching fulfilment of the whole.
1:24: 24.] This explanatory notice is not very clear. Lücke, with De Wette, refers it to the apparent hostility of the enquiry which follows, though it can hardly be thought more hostile than the preceding. Might it not rather throw light on the particular question about baptizing, the Pharisees being most precise of all about ceremonies and lustrations?
1:26: 26.] Their question shews probably that they did not interpret Isa. xl. 3 as referring to any herald of the Messiah specifically; they regarded baptism itself as a significant token of the approach of the Messianic Kingdom, and so asked, why baptizest thou, if thou be not he?
1:29:
29–34.] Second witness borne by John to Jesus, the day after.

29.] The question whether this testimony of the Baptist is identical with that given by the three Evangelists, especially by Luke (iii. 16), is, after all, of no great importance. The whole series of transactions here recorded, from ver. 15 onwards, certainly happened after that event — before that event John did not know Him as ὁ ἐρχόμενος: and μέσος ὑμῶν στήκει (ver. 26) shews that he had by then come to recognize Him; whereas the testimony in Luke iii. 16 is certainly before the baptism. Since his mission was to proclaim Him, it is not only probable but necessary to suppose that he delivered this testimony often, and under varying circumstances: before the baptism, in the form given by Luke; and after it in this form, οὑτός ἦν ὄν εἶπον (ver. 15), where his former testimony is distinctly referred to.

ὁ ἀμνὸς τοῦ θεοῦ: this title combines the idea of the Paschal lamb, sent of God and slain for sin, with that of the suffering and innocent servant of God in Isa. liii., on whom the iniquity of all should be laid. τὴν ἄμαρτίαν τοῦ κόσμου, the sin, collectively — the whole mass and principle of sin which lieth on the world. αἰρων, in the sense of taking away sin and its guilt by expiation (see Exod. xxxiv. 7; Levit. x. 17; Num. v. 15) — He taketh it away by the bearing and removal of it in Himself. If the Lamb is to suffer the burden of the sins of the world, and to take away sin and its guilt by expiation, this result must be accomplished by the offering of Himself.
1:30: 30.] On this apparent discrepancy, between οὐχ ὑαα ἰδειν αὐτόν here and St. Matthew's narrative, see note on Matt. iii. 14. Both accounts are entirely consistent with the supposition that John had been from youth upwards acquainted with our Lord, and indeed may in some sense have believed Him to be the Christ — but, until the special sign appointed to him for recognizing Him as such was given, he had, like the rest of the people, no certain knowledge of Him.
1:35:
35–43.] On account of the testimony of John, first Andrew, and another of his disciples, and through Andrew, Simon Peter, become acquainted with Jesus.

35.] τῇ ἐπαύριον, the day after that on which the witness in vv. 29–34 had been borne — what the two disciples had then heard seems to have made a powerful impression on their minds.
1:37: 37.] ἡκολούθησαν is not to be understood here in the narrower sense which it bears when it means to have left all and followed Him; here only of mechanical accompaniment.
1:39: 39.] ὁρα δεκάτη, i.e. 4 p.m., according to the Jewish reckoning — not, as some have thought, 10 a.m., according to the Roman. Our Evangelist appears always to reckon according to the Jewish method (see ch. iv. 6, 52; xix. 14, and especially ch. xi. 9); and the division of the day into twelve equal hours was, even among the Jews, the popular, not the civil, way of computing time.
1:40: 40.] One of the two which heard John speak, and followed him, was Andrew, Simon Peter's brother — the other, left unnamed, being generally held, from the studied reticence usual in this Gospel regarding the writer himself, to have been the Evangelist.
1:41: 41.] πρώτος, first, of the two — before the other did so: the immediate impulse, on finding the Messiah himself, is to bring his own brother to the same knowledge.
1:42: 42.] κηφᾶς, the Aramaic for a stone, here first given by our Lord, before the formal bestowal of the same name, Peter, recorded at a later period of his call (see Matt. xvi. 18). The Greek name Peter became the prevalent one in the apostolic Church very soon; Paul uses both names indiscriminately.
1:44:
44–51.] The calling of Philip and Nathanael.

44.] τῇ ἐπαύρ.] Apparently the day after the naming of Peter, and so the fourth day after ver. 19. Our Lord is on the point of setting out from the valley of the Jordan into Galilee, and finds Philip, with whom there is every reason to believe He was already acquainted (see ver. 46). Here Jesus Himself calls a disciple for the first time; but ἀκολούθει does not bear here its strict apostolic sense, since the going to search for others among those already mentioned shews that they were not yet inseparably attached as followers.
1:46:
46.] It does not appear where Nathanael was found, but he is described elsewhere (ch. xxi. 2) as being of Cana in Galilee; and as Jesus is found there soon after (ch. ii. 1), it is probable the call took place in that neighbourhood. Nathanael is mentioned only in this Gospel; and as his name is nowhere found in the catalogues of the twelve, while Philip is associated in three of them with Bartholomew, it has been supposed (though this is mere conjecture) that Nathanael and Bartholomew were the same person.

τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Ἀωσήφ.] This expression seems to shew previous acquaintance on Philip's part with Jesus. No stress can be laid, as has been unfairly done by some, on Jesus being called by Philip the son of Joseph, as though this indicated that the history of His miraculous birth was unknown to John; Philip simply expresses the ordinary, prevailing belief, as Olshausen also remarks.
1:47: 47.] The meaning of this question is simpler than at first sight appears. It is impossible that Nathanael, himself a Galilean, could speak from any feeling of contempt for Galileans generally, and there is no evidence that Nazareth was held in any special contempt among them. He alludes rather to the smallness and insignificance of the town, which finds no place either in the Old Testament or in Josephus.
1:48: 48.] The Evangelist certainly intends a supernatural insight by the Lord into Nathanael's character to be understood here, with probably no reference at all to the question Nathanael had just asked — to suppose that Jesus merely overheard that question is one of those gratuitous assumptions which the very Commentators who insist on it are usually the first to disallow elsewhere. ἀληθῶς: an Israelite who truly answers to the inner and honourable meaning of the name — of simple and honest mind, without dissimulation or self-seeking.
1:49: 49.] The question πόθεν με γινώσεις is one of astonishment, not yet, perhaps, of suspicion of anything supernatural; our Lord's answer first opens this to him. Whether ὄντα ὑπὸ τ. συκ. belongs to φανερωθῇναι or to εἶδόν σε is doubtful, did not ver. 51 decide for the latter construction. The declaration that Jesus had seen him there at once brings the conviction here expressed; this would not have been the case unless the sight had been evidently and unquestionably supernatural.
1:50: 50.] ‘Thou art the Messiah’: see Ps. ii. 7; ch. xi. 27; Matt. xvi. 16; Luke xxii. 70. Olshausen maintains that ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ was not, of itself, a Jewish appellation for the Messiah — on account of the Jews taking up stones to cast at Jesus when He so called Himself (ch. x. 33). But, as Lücke observes, it was not for using the title in itself, but for using it in a close and literal sense which was unintelligible to them, that offence was taken.
1:51: 51.] Our Lord says this not in blame, but rather in praise of the simple and honest expression of Nathanael's conviction; principally, however, to shew him that if he believed by reason of this comparatively small proof of divine power, his faith would increase from strength to strength at the greater proofs which should from that time forward be given. ἀμὴν ἀμήν is peculiar to John; the other Evangelists use ἀμήν once only as an asseveration. ὑμῖν: these words are spoken to all the disciples present, not only to Nathanael. The glories of the period now beginning, and at that day not yet completed, are described: not the outward, visible opening of the material heavens, nor any actual ascent or descent of angels in the sight of men, but the series of glories which were about to be unfolded in His Person and Work from that time forward.
